'''Edward David Goldberg''' (August 2, 1921 – March 7, 2008) was a [[Chemical oceanography|marine chemist]], known for his studies of [[Marine pollution|pollution in the oceans]].

==Biography==
Goldberg was born on August 2, 1921, in [[Sacramento, California]]. He received his B.S. in [[chemistry]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1942, and then, after serving in the Navy during [[World War II]], did his graduate studies under the supervision of [[Harrison Brown]] at the [[University of Chicago]], where he received his Ph.D. in chemistry in 1949. For the rest of his life, he worked as a professor of chemistry at the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] at the [[University of California, San Diego]]. He died March 7, 2008, in [[Encinitas, California]].<ref name="lat">[https://www.latimes.com/news/obituaries/la-me-goldberg17mar17,1,4943052.story Obituary of Goldberg], ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', March 17, 2008, p. B7.</ref><ref name="scripps obit">[http://scrippsnews.ucsd.edu/Releases/?releaseID=888 Obituary Notice; Pioneer in Marine Chemistry and Ocean Pollution Research: Edward Goldberg] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130514230943/http://scrippsnews.ucsd.edu/Releases/?releaseID=888 |date=2013-05-14 }}, [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]], March 11, 2008.</ref>

The director of Scripps, Tony Haymet, wrote about him that<ref name="scripps obit"/>
{{cquote|Ed Goldberg earned the reputation not only as an extraordinary marine chemist, but also as an engaging professor who truly inspired his students. He was always willing to tackle the tough issues facing the marine environment and our harbors and seas are better off due to Ed's enduring dedication and commitment.}}

==Research==
Goldberg wrote more than 225 research papers and a number of books, largely concerning ocean [[geochemistry]], marine life in coastal waters, and man's impact on the ocean.

One of Goldberg's earliest studies on ocean pollution concerned [[sewage]] in [[Santa Monica Bay]]. Goldberg warned of pollution's risk to all ocean life at the 1969 [[American Geophysical Union]] conference.
{{cquote|Will it alter the ocean as a resource? Will we lose the ocean?|author=Edward Goldberg<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1969/12/21/archives/scientists-caution-on-changes-in-climate-as-result-of-pollution.html|work=The New York Times|date=December 21, 1969|title=Scientists Caution on Changes In Climate as Result of Pollution|author=UPI}}</ref> }}

Later, in the 1970s, Goldberg began the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]]-funded Mussel Watch program, which measured ocean pollution by its effects on [[shellfish]].<ref name="lat"/><ref name="scripps obit"/><ref>{{citation|title=The Mussel Watch|first9=Eric|last10=Gamble|first10=Eric|last9=Schneider|first8=William|last8=Robertson|first7=Robert W.|last7=Risebrough|first6=Patrick L.|last6=Parker|first5=John H.|last5=Martin|last1=Goldberg|first4=George|first1=E. D.|last2=Bowen|last4=Harvey|first2=V. T.|last3=Farrington|first3=J. W.|journal=Environmental Conservation|volume=5|issue=2|pages=101–125|year=1978|doi=10.1017/S0376892900005555|bibcode=1978EnvCo...5..101G |s2cid=85937128 |display-authors=8}}.</ref> His studies led him to push for a ban on [[tributyltin]], a chemical that was used in [[Bottom paint|ship paint]] for its toxic effects on [[barnacle]]s but that was poisoning the [[mussel]]s in [[San Diego Bay]].<ref name="lat"/><ref name="scripps obit"/><ref>"Scientist Calls for TBT Ban; Boat Paint Chemical Seen as a Threat to Marine Life", Janny Scott and David Smollar, ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', July 6, 1986.</ref> Goldberg also published highly cited works on [[colloid]]s in ocean water<ref>{{citation|title=Occurrence of small colloids in sea water|last1=Wells|first1=M. L.|last2=Goldberg|first2=E. D.|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=353|pages=342–344|year=1991|doi=10.1038/353342a0|issue=6342|bibcode=1991Natur.353..342W|s2cid=4352131}}.</ref> and on pollution from [[fossil fuel]] consumption.<ref>{{citation|title=Fossil Fuel Combustion and the Major Sedimentary Cycle|last1=Bertine|first1=K. K.|last2=Goldberg|first2=E. D.|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|year=1971|volume=173|issue=3993|pages=233–235|doi=10.1126/science.173.3993.233|pmid=17741418|bibcode=1971Sci...173..233B|s2cid=8675195}}; {{citation|title=Black carbon in the environment|last=Goldberg|first=E. D.|publisher=Wiley and Sons|year=1985|series=Environmental Science and Technology Series|isbn=978-0-471-81979-0}}.</ref>

A significant innovation in Goldberg's research was the suggestion, implemented in Mussel Watch and now commonplace in marine chemistry, of using mussels to measure pollutant levels. For instance, Mills writes, "Measurements of metals by direct chemical analysis in water and sediment are
limited in reliability. Consequently, after the initial suggestion by Goldberg (1975), many studies have utilised mussels to assess metals in the environment. Mussels have been suggested to be the ideal [[bioindicator]] organism in biomonitoring studies due to their sessile filter-feeding life style, coupled with their abilities to accumulate metals to much higher concentrations than those found in water and to not metabolise metals appreciably."<ref>{{citation|title=The use of transplanted brown mussels (Perna perna) as indicators of marine health in Richards Bay harbour|last=Mills|first=Kerry Anne|series=Ph.D. thesis|url=http://etd.rau.ac.za/theses/available/etd-09012006-094821/|publisher=[[University of Johannesburg]]|year=2006|pages=4–2}}{{Dead link|date=August 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}.</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 1984 he won the first [[B H Ketchum Award|Bostwick H. Ketchum Award]], given by the [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]], both for his leadership in environmental quality research and for his efforts to translate that research into policy.<ref>[http://www.whoi.edu/page.do?pid=7616&tid=282&cid=23307 First Ketchum Award Presented to Internationally-Known Marine Geochemist], [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]] Newsletter, April/May 1984.</ref> In 1989 he won the [[Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement]] for his work on marine pollution,<ref name="lat"/><ref>"Crutzen, Goldberg are Tyler Prize recipients", Daily News of Los Angeles, May 21, 1989.</ref> and the Roger Revelle Award of the San Diego Oceans Foundation.<ref>[http://www.sdoceans.org/top_about_roger_revelle_award.html Roger Revelle Award] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080704124903/http://www.sdoceans.org/top_about_roger_revelle_award.html |date=2008-07-04 }}, San Diego Oceans Foundation.</ref> In 1999, the [[American Society of Limnology and Oceanography]] gave Goldberg the first Ruth Patrick Award for Environmental Problem Solving in the Aquatic Sciences.<ref name="scripps obit"/> Goldberg was also a [[Fellow]] of the [[Meteoritical Society]]<ref>[http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1953Metic...1...96R Notices from the Secretary of the Meteoritical Society], ''Meteoritics and Planetary Science'', vol. 1, p. 96, 1953.</ref> and a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="scripps obit"/><ref>"Academy of Sciences Picks 59 Members and 12 Associates", ''[[The New York Times]]'', April 27, 1980.</ref>
